(CNN) -- The search will continue until at least Friday night for 16 people missing since Thursday morning when a helicopter carrying them to an offshore oil platform ditched in the Atlantic Ocean off Newfoundland, Canadian officials said. A helicopter made an emergency crash landing off Newfoundland en route to Hibernia oil field on Thursday. One survivor, identified as Robert Decker, was found and taken to a hospital, but efforts to find more survivors had proven fruitless, said Maj. Denis McGuire of the Rescue Coordination Center in Halifax, Nova Scotia. The body of one person, who has not been identified publicly, also was pulled from the water. There were 18 people aboard the helicopter when it went down, about 30 nautical miles from St. John's. "All we've got is the debris field," McGuire said. "There are no indications of any [more] survivors, but the search will continue." The water is 400 feet deep at the site where the helicopter hit the water, he said. Helicopters and ships were scouring the debris field Thursday evening, and search-and-rescue technicians were planning to use night-vision goggles and flares overnight. The debris filled a six-mile area, said Jeri Grychowski of the Rescue Coordination Centre in Halifax. Officials became aware that the helicopter was having problems shortly after 9:10 a.m., when the pilot declared a mayday, McGuire said. "They declared their mayday and then they hit the water or landed in the water approximately eight minutes later," he said. About 25 minutes later, a helicopter arrived and discovered the survivor, the body, the overturned helicopter and two empty life rafts, he said. Those aboard should have have been wearing survival suits that would have kept them dry and were equipped with lights and personal locator beacons, but the suits have not helped searchers. "We have not received any signals whatsoever," McGuire said. The suits theoretically would allow wearers to survive 24 hours in the freezing waters -- or until about 9 a.m. Friday -- but the search effort was to continue well beyond that. "We will continue to search until there's absolutely no chance that any survivors will be located," he said. "Until last light [Friday]." At that time, based on water temperature and the size of the search area, officials will decide whether to continue the effort, he said. Early in the day, high winds and seas hampered the search, but by late afternoon, the weather had improved, though seas were still about 13 to 16 feet (4 to 5 meters) and winds were at about 40 knots (46 mph). The survivor was taken to the Health Sciences Center in St. John's, Newfoundland. The helicopter had been heading to the Hibernia offshore oil platform when it went down in what Grychowski called a controlled emergency crash landing. The pilot reported some technical malfunctions before the crash and radioed that he was turning the chopper around, said Rick Burt of Cougar Helicopters -- the operator of the S-92 Sikorsky copter.

**Search underway after helicopter carrying oil workers crashes off Newfoundland coast**

By Paula Newton and Eric Levenson, CNN
Updated 3:14 PM EDT, Thursday

**ST. JOHN’S, Newfoundland (CNN) —** A massive search and rescue operation is underway in the frigid waters of the North Atlantic after a commercial helicopter carrying offshore oil workers crashed Thursday morning off the coast of Newfoundland, Canadian authorities said.

The aircraft, which had 18 people on board—16 passengers and two crew members—was en route from St. John’s to the Hibernia oil platform, located roughly 315 kilometers (195 miles) east of the provincial capital, when it issued a distress call and went down.

According to the Joint Rescue Coordination Centre (JRCC) in Halifax, the helicopter transmitted a Mayday signal before losing radar contact approximately 85 nautical miles offshore. 

Searchers have located a debris field and an unoccupied liferaft in the area where the signal was lost, officials confirmed to CNN. 

**'A race against time'**

Multiple air and sea assets have been deployed to the site, including Canadian Coast Guard vessels, RCAF Cormorant search-and-rescue helicopters, and a Hercules C-130 aircraft. Commercial supply vessels operating near the Hibernia field have also been diverted to assist in the recovery efforts.

"We are currently executing a full-scale search and rescue response," said Lt. Cmdr. Mark Davis, a spokesperson for JRCC Halifax. "Our primary focus is locating survivors. Given the water temperatures in the North Atlantic at this time of year, this is a race against time."

Ocean temperatures in the area are hovering around 4 degrees Celsius (39 degrees Fahrenheit), making immersion suits critical for survival. High swells and heavy sea fog in the Grand Banks region are currently complicating visibility for air crews, authorities noted.

**Oil company activates emergency response**

The helicopter was operated by a regional offshore transport provider under contract for the platform's operator. 

In a brief statement Thursday afternoon, the consortium managing the Hibernia platform expressed deep concern for the crew and passengers.

"Our immediate priority is the safety and well-being of the personnel on board and supporting their families," the statement read. "We are working closely with the Joint Rescue Coordination Centre and federal authorities in the ongoing search efforts."

A family information center has been established at the St. John's International Airport, where relatives of those on board have begun gathering to await updates.

**A critical offshore hub**

The Hibernia gravity-based structure, which began production in 1997, is one of Canada’s largest offshore oil projects. Located in the harsh environment of the Grand Banks, the platform relies heavily on daily helicopter transport to ferry workers to and from the island of Newfoundland.

Offshore helicopter travel in the region is subject to strict safety protocols due to the challenging weather patterns, thick fog, and treacherous marine conditions common to the region.

Canadian safety officials, including the Transportation Safety Board (TSB), confirmed they are monitoring the situation and deploying a team of investigators to St. John's to prepare for an inquiry once rescue operations conclude.

**BREAKING: Massive Search and Rescue Operation Underway After Offshore Helicopter Crashes Off Newfoundland Coast**

**ST. JOHN’S, Newfoundland and Labrador —** A major search and rescue operation is racing against the clock in the frigid waters of the North Atlantic after a commercial helicopter carrying 16 people crashed off the coast of Newfoundland on Thursday afternoon.

The aircraft, a Sikorsky S-92 operated by Atlantic Offshore Aviation, was en route to the White Rose oil field, approximately 180 kilometers (110 miles) east of St. John’s, when it issued a Mayday call at approximately 2:15 p.m. local time. Shortly after, the aircraft’s Emergency Locator Transmitter (ELT) was activated, and radio contact was lost.

Fourteen workers and two crew members were on board, officials confirmed. 

The Joint Rescue Coordination Centre (JRCC) in Halifax has launched a full-scale response, deploying Royal Canadian Air Force (RCAF) CH-149 Cormorant search and rescue helicopters and a CC-130H Hercules aircraft from 103 Search and Rescue Squadron based in Gander. 

The Canadian Coast Guard vessel *CCGS Leonard J. Cowley* has been diverted to the scene, along with two nearby commercial supply ships, which were the first to arrive at the last known coordinates of the aircraft.

Searchers face extreme environmental conditions. Officials report water temperatures hovering near 1°C (34°F), air temperatures below freezing, wind gusts exceeding 40 knots, and sea swells of up to five meters (16 feet), creating a critical window for survival.

"Our absolute focus is on locating the passengers and crew," said RCAF Maj. Trevor Reid, a spokesperson for JRCC Halifax. "Rescuers are battling heavy seas and reduced visibility, but all available military, coast guard, and civilian assets in the area have been tasked to the search zone."

As nightfall approaches, search aircraft are dropping illumination flares over a debris field that was spotted roughly 12 kilometers from the offshore rig's helipad. 

According to military sources, at least two fully inflated immersion life rafts have been spotted in the water, but rescue swimmers have not yet been able to confirm if survivors are aboard due to severe wave action. Offshore oil workers in the region are required to wear high-tech thermal immersion suits, which offer extended protection against hypothermia, providing a critical lifeline in such extreme conditions.

Offshore energy operator Equinor, which contracted the flight, released a brief statement confirming it has activated its emergency response team and is providing support to the families of those on board. A family reception center has been established at the St. John’s International Airport.

Premier of Newfoundland and Labrador, Andrew Furey, addressed the unfolding crisis on social media Thursday evening: "Our thoughts and prayers are with the passengers, crew, and their families during this harrowing time. We remain hopeful as our brave first responders and rescue crews work tirelessly in difficult conditions."

**ST. JOHN'S, Newfoundland (CNN)** — A harrowing race against time in the sub-zero waters of the North Atlantic has turned into a scene of profound grief off the coast of eastern Canada. 

As search and rescue crews scour a debris field 35 nautical miles east of St. John’s, Newfoundland, officials are piecing together the final, desperate minutes of Cougar Helicopters Flight 91—a passenger flight carrying offshore oil workers that ditched into the ocean on Thursday morning.

Out of the 18 people on board the Sikorsky S-92A aircraft, only one survivor has been pulled alive from the frigid waters. One body has been recovered, and military personnel, the Canadian Coast Guard, and local offshore vessels continue a grim, non-stop search for the remaining 16 passengers and crew.

Here is a comprehensive breakdown of the terrifying timeline, the brutal environment confronting rescuers, and the latest statements from search coordinators.

---

### **The Timeline: A Rapid Mechanical Failure**

Flight 91 took off from St. John’s International Airport shortly after 9:00 a.m. local time, bound for the Hibernia oil platform and the SeaRose floating production, storage, and offloading (FPSO) vessel. Onboard were 16 passengers—contractors and employees for oil giants Chevron, Husky Energy, and Petro-Canada—and two Cougar Helicopters crew members.

According to flight logs and radar data released by air traffic control and search coordinators, the routine flight turned critical within minutes:

*   **9:18 a.m. NT:** Flight 91 departs St. John’s, heading east over the North Atlantic.
*   **9:40 a.m. NT:** The flight crew contacts air traffic control reporting a severe mechanical anomaly—specifically, zero oil pressure in the main gearbox. 
*   **9:43 a.m. NT:** The pilot formally declares a **"Mayday"** emergency. The crew announces its intention to abort the mission, turn the aircraft around, and attempt an immediate return to St. John’s. The helicopter begins a controlled descent from its cruising altitude of approximately 9,000 feet down to 800 feet.
*   **9:55 a.m. NT:** Radio contact and radar signal are abruptly lost. The aircraft vanishes from radar screens roughly 35 nautical miles (65 kilometers) east-southeast of St. John’s. No further distress signals or beacon transmissions are received from the helicopter.

---

### **Treacherous Search Conditions**

Rescue operations were triggered immediately, but crews faced some of the most unforgiving marine conditions on the planet.

The water temperature at the crash site was recorded at a bone-chilling **0 degrees Celsius (32 degrees Fahrenheit)**, with air temperatures hovering near freezing. At these temperatures, an unprotected human body succumbs to hypothermia within minutes.

While all workers traveling to Newfoundland’s offshore platforms are required to wear specialized high-tech immersion suits designed to retain body heat and float, experts note that even with these suits, survival times are strictly limited in severe Atlantic swells.

"The North Atlantic in March is an utterly hostile environment," said CNN aviation and marine safety analyst Capt. Mitchell Hayes. "You are dealing with ocean swells between two to three meters (6 to 10 feet), rising wind speeds, and localized fog banks that drastically reduce visibility for aircrews searching from above."

Heavy seas and scattered sea fog forced low-flying search aircraft to rely heavily on forward-looking infrared (FLIR) optics and visual spotters hanging out of open helicopter doors in freezing wind chills.

---

### **Official Statements from Search and Rescue Coordinators**

The Joint Rescue Coordination Centre (JRCC) in Halifax, Nova Scotia, took immediate command of the massive multi-agency response, deploying Canadian Forces aircraft, Coast Guard vessels, and civilian ships operating in the grand banks oil fields.

Speaking from JRCC Halifax, **Maj. Denis McGuire**, a spokesperson for the Canadian Forces search and rescue operations, detailed the swift deployment of military assets:

> *"Immediately upon notification of the lost radar contact at 09:55 hours, JRCC Halifax taskings were issued. We deployed two CH-149 Cormorant rescue helicopters and a CC-130 Hercules aircraft out of 103 Search and Rescue Squadron in Gander. Furthermore, the Canadian Coast Guard Vessel Leonard J. Cowley was redirected to the scene alongside local commercial supply vessels already in the area."*

Addressing the severe weather and survival window, Maj. McGuire emphasized that operations were initially treated entirely as a rescue effort:

> *"Our primary objective from minute one has been life preservation. The water temperatures are extraordinarily low, but the passengers were equipped with thermal immersion suits. We operated under the assumption that we were looking for survivors in the water. Every available sensor, radar, and visual asset was focused on that debris field."*

By mid-afternoon, rescue teams located a floating life raft, but JRCC coordinators confirmed a heartbreaking detail: **the raft was empty.** 

Shortly thereafter, a CH-149 Cormorant helicopter spotted two individuals in the water. Search crews lowered a SAR technician into the rough waves, successfully winching one survivor—identified as 28-year-old Robert Decker—and one deceased individual out of the ocean. 

Decker was airlifted directly to the Health Sciences Centre in St. John’s, where doctors report he remains in critical but stable condition, suffering from severe hypothermia and trauma injuries.

In a evening press briefing, **Lt. Navy Paul Pendergast**, public affairs officer for JRCC Halifax, provided an update on the ongoing surface search:

> *"We have located a significant debris field, including oil slicks, personal effects, and structural remnants of the helicopter. The Canadian Coast Guard ship Leonard J. Cowley has arrived on scene and assumed surface command. The search will continue through the night using night-vision equipment, illumination flares from our Hercules aircraft, and high-intensity searchlights from surface vessels. We are not giving up hope, but conditions on the water remain exceptionally challenging."*

---

### **A Region in Mourning**

Back in St. John’s, a heavy pall has fallen over the close-knit offshore energy community. Families of the workers gathered at a designated center near the airport, waiting in agonizing silence for updates on their loved ones.

Cougar Helicopters, a primary transport contractor for the Newfoundland offshore industry, grounded its remaining fleet of S-92 helicopters pending an immediate review. 

The Transportation Safety Board of Canada (TSB) has dispatched an expert team of investigators to St. John’s. Their focus will center on why the main gearbox suffered a catastrophic loss of oil pressure, and whether the crew attempted a controlled ditching on the water or suffered a sudden, violent loss of control before impact.

As night falls over the North Atlantic, searchlight beams cut through the dark, cold spray 35 miles off the Canadian coast—where the search for 16 missing workers continues against staggering odds.

*Reporting by CNN in St. John's, Newfoundland.*

According to air traffic control logs, the emergency unfolded rapidly. At approximately 9:40 a.m. local time, the pilots issued a Mayday call, reporting zero oil pressure in the main gearbox. The crew immediately turned the helicopter back toward St. John's and requested a descent to a lower altitude. Minutes later, at 9:55 a.m., radar and radio contact with the aircraft was abruptly lost.

### Rapid Military and Civilian Response

The Joint Rescue Coordination Centre (JRCC) in Halifax immediately initiated a massive, multi-agency search-and-rescue response. 

Within minutes of the signal loss, a Royal Canadian Air Force (RCAF) CH-149 Cormorant helicopter and a CC-130 Hercules aircraft were scrambled from 103 Search and Rescue Squadron based at CFB Gander. Additional military air assets were dispatched from CFB Greenwood in Nova Scotia.

Civilian vessels in the area were immediately diverted to the crash site. The *Atlantic Osprey*, an offshore supply vessel, was among the first surface ships to respond, alongside the Canadian Coast Guard vessel *CCGS Leonard J. Cowley*, which was tasked with coordinating the surface search.

"We deployed every available asset the moment radar contact was lost," said a spokesperson for JRCC Halifax. "Our primary focus remains on locating survivors in what are extremely harsh operational conditions."

### A Miraculous Rescue Clinging to Hope

Roughly an hour and a half after the helicopter hit the water, the crew of an RCAF Cormorant search-and-rescue helicopter spotted a debris field floating on the ocean surface, along with oil slicks and red emergency dye.

Amidst the ocean swells, rescue personnel spotted a single individual floating in a thermal survival suit. A SAR technician was lowered into the ocean via hoist to retrieve the victim, who was conscious but suffering from severe trauma and advanced hypothermia. 

The survivor—later identified as 28-year-old offshore worker Robert Decker—was rushed directly to the Health Sciences Centre in St. John’s, where he remains in critical but stable condition in intensive care.

However, the relief of finding a survivor was quickly overshadowed by grim discoveries shortly thereafter. Search crews located two empty, automatically deployed liferafts floating in the debris field, suggesting that the aircraft hit the water with immense force, leaving those inside little to no time to execute a controlled evacuation into the rafts. 

Floating debris—including luggage, flight gear, and pieces of the helicopter's fuselage—has been recovered by the *Atlantic Osprey*, but no other survivors have been found.

### Battling the Frigid Atlantic

As night falls over the search area, rescue crews are racing against a brutal clock. Ocean temperatures at the crash site are hovering near 0°C (32°F), with air temperatures just above freezing. 

While all passengers were wearing high-tech neoprene immersion suits designed to prolong survival in freezing water, experts note that the window for survival in such extreme conditions, even with protective gear, drops dramatically after a few hours—especially if individuals suffered physical trauma during the impact.

Waves at the search site are reported to be two to three meters high, complicated by patchy fog and reduced visibility. 

### Shockwaves Through the Energy Sector

The incident has sent shockwaves through the province of Newfoundland and Labrador, where the offshore oil industry is a vital economic engine and a tightly knit community. 

Families of the passengers gathered at a hotel near St. John's airport, desperately waiting for updates from Cougar Helicopters and government officials. Premier Danny Williams issued a brief statement expressing the province’s collective grief and anxiety.

"This is a dark day for Newfoundland and Labrador," Williams said. "Our thoughts and prayers are entirely with the workers, the crew, and their families who are waiting for news. We hold onto hope, but we prepare our hearts for the worst."

Cougar Helicopters has grounded its remaining fleet of S-92 aircraft pending an initial review of the incident.

### Investigation Underway

The Transportation Safety Board of Canada (TSB) has assembled a team of investigators who are preparing to head to St. John’s. The team’s primary objective will be to determine why the helicopter experienced a sudden loss of main gearbox pressure and whether the aircraft attempted a controlled ditching or suffered a catastrophic structural failure before hitting the water.

For now, the operation remains officially classified as a search-and-rescue mission. The RCAF Hercules aircraft will drop flares throughout the night to illuminate the water, allowing Coast Guard and offshore vessels to continue sweeping the 100-square-mile search grid until dawn.
